# Missing data

::: {.question}
**How are your missing values currently represented?**

- [Blank cells / already shown as NA](06-missing.qmd#sec-missing-decide)
- [Coded as numbers (e.g., -99, 999) or text like "missing"](06-missing.qmd#sec-missing-recode)
- [I'm not sure — help me check first](06-missing.qmd#sec-missing-check)
:::

## Check how missingness is coded {#sec-missing-check}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `naniar` `dplyr`
:::

Psychology surveys often use out-of-range numbers (999, -99, -1) to mean 'missing' rather than a true blank cell. Spotting these before analysis is essential — otherwise R will treat them as real scores.

```r
library(naniar)
miss_var_summary(survey_raw)   # official NAs per column
vis_miss(survey_raw)

# eyeball one column's actual values for suspicious codes
library(dplyr)
survey_raw |> count(mood_rating)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Check your study's codebook — researchers usually document which numeric code means 'missing' for each measure.
:::

## Convert coded missing values to real NA {#sec-missing-recode}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `naniar`
:::

naniar's replace_with_na() turns specific values into proper NA, so dplyr/tidyr functions recognise them as missing instead of as real data.

```r
library(naniar)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  replace_with_na(replace = list(
    age = c(-99, 999),
    mood_rating = c(-99)
  ))

# or apply the same missing code to every column at once
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  replace_with_na_all(condition = ~ .x %in% c(-99, 999))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Keep a note of which codes you replaced — it belongs in your methods write-up, not just your script.
:::

::: {.next-steps}
**Where to next:**

## Decide what to do about missing values {#sec-missing-decide}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `tidyr` `dplyr` `naniar`
:::

Once missing values are properly coded as NA, you have a few options depending on your design.

```r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

# remove rows with ANY missing value
survey_complete <- survey_raw |> drop_na()

# remove rows missing on specific key variables only
survey_complete <- survey_raw |> drop_na(age, condition)

# flag participants with a lot of missing data instead of dropping automatically
library(naniar)
survey_raw |>
  mutate(pct_missing = rowMeans(is.na(across(everything()))) * 100) |>
  filter(pct_missing > 50)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Don't drop_na() the whole dataset by default — think about whether missingness is random or meaningful (e.g. someone quit the survey early) before deciding how to handle it.
:::
